articles.title: Pete Hegseth Prepares To Join Elite Club (Of The Impeached)
articles.content:
With Rep. Thomas Massie expected to force a vote to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, how many times has a cabinet secretary been impeached by the House of Representatives?

Hint: We aren’t asking about the outcome in the Senate… for example, if the Senate dismissed the articles of impeachment as unconstitutional without hearing the case, that would still count (so that should tell you that the answer is at least once).

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: Legal Ethics Roundup: DOJ Ethics Probe, Bar Exam Tampering, AI Billing Limits, TX Reconsiders ABA Accreditation Council, Biglaw Shakeup, AI Privilege & More
articles.content:
Ed. note: Please welcome Renee Knake Jefferson back to the pages of Above the Law. Subscribe to her Substack, Legal Ethics Roundup, here.
Hello (again) from DC. I’m back for a conference on college athletics governance, one of several governance and ethics issues on my calendar this week. More on that below.
#1 “Judge Taps Ex-Prosecutor to Probe Lawyer Conduct in Trump Golf Course Fight.” From The Washington Post: “A federal judge said Saturday that she intends to appoint Jessie K. Liu, the former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia during President Donald Trump’s first term, to investigate whether Justice and Interior Department lawyers committed ethical violations in the legal fight over the administration’s plans for East Potomac Golf Links. U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes identified Liu as her choice to serve as a special master, an outside investigator who would assist the court in examining the government’s conduct in the case.” Read more here (gift link).
#2 “Arkansas Court Official Tampered With Bar Exam Results, Prosecutor Says.” From Reuters: “A former Arkansas court administrator is facing felony charges after an investigation uncovered ‘extensive irregularities’ with bar exam results from 2020 to 2025, prosecutors said. Nancie Givens, who resigned her position as executive director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas’ Office of Professional Programs in February, faces 65 felony counts of tampering with a public record, Sixth Judicial District Prosecuting Attorney Will Jones announced on Thursday.” Read more here.
#3 “New York State Bar Association Tells Lawyers Not to Bill for Time Saved by AI.” From the ABA Journal: “The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use them.” Read more here.
#4 “Judge Questions Federal Role in Ed Martin Ethics Case.” From Law360: “A D.C. federal judge struggled Tuesday to see how he could preside over a state attorney ethics proceeding if U.S. pardon attorney Ed Martin gets his way and keeps the case.” Read more here.
#5 “Texas’ Next Top Justice Wants to Return to ABA Accreditation.” From Bloomberg Law: “Texas’ next chief justice of the state supreme court, Democrat Maggie Ellis, wants the state to again let the American Bar Association accredit law schools. Earlier this year, the all-Republican court voted to end the state’s decades long relationship over the ABA’s diversity, equity, and inclusion requirements. The move tracked attacks on the group by the Trump administration and other Republican states. But after four Democrats, including Ellis, unseated GOP incumbents Tuesday, she said she wants to revisit that decision when she joins and leads the nine-justice court in January. ‘My hope is that we’re able to each share ideas and the new supreme court can look at it and not base it on following in the footsteps of initiatives of the governor,’ Ellis told Bloomberg Law on Thursday.” Read more here.
#6 “Ex-Sidley Associate Becomes First Gen Z Woman Elected to Congress.” From Law.com: “Melat Kiros had worked at Sidley as a first-year associate in New York for about a year when the law firm terminated her in November 2023 for penning an open letter on Medium titled, ‘Dear Law Firms.’” Read more here.
#7 “The Ethics Rules Behind Weil Gotshal’s ‘Partner Run.’” From The Wall Street Journal: “Bans on outside ownership and noncompete agreements make it hard for law firms to innovate—and sometimes even to survive.” Read more here (gift link).
#8 “Government Backs ‘Comprehensive Review’ of Legal Services Regulation.” From LegalFutures (UK): “The government is to undertake a ‘comprehensive review’ of whether legal services regulation remains fit for purpose, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) revealed today. Legal services minister Sarah Sackman said she agreed with the conclusion of the Lloyd review earlier this year that ‘significant change is needed to strengthen the effectiveness of legal services regulation.’” Read more here.
#9 “Is Legal Advice Developed By Or With An AI System Legally Privileged?” From JD Supra: “A year ago, we published an analysis on legal privilege and AI. At the time, there was limited judicial or regulatory guidance on how using AI in legal work might affect privilege, and no case law on the issue, so we took a first principles approach. In this article, we revisit this topic with the benefit of recent case law in key jurisdictions, judicial commentary and regulatory guidance. As before, we concentrate on the impact of AI on legal advice privilege over litigation privilege, where the impact of the use of AI may have a different result.” Read more here.
#10 “The New Hot Job in Law Doesn’t Require a J.D.” From The New York Times: “Big law firms, legal tech vendors, and in-house legal departments at companies like Microsoft and Nvidia are all hiring legal engineers, a new position for lawyers with A.I. skills.” Read more here (gift link).
This week takes me to Washington, DC, Springfield, MO, and Palm Springs, CA. In DC, I’ll attend The Governance Challenge in College Athletics, a conference hosted by the Association of Governing Boards of Universities and Colleges (AGB). I was appointed to AGB’s Council of Public Board Leaders this fall.
Then I’m off to Springfield, where I was born and where many members of my extended family still live, for a special Veterans Day event honoring relatives who served in World War II.
My week concludes in Palm Springs for an ABA Accreditation Council meeting. You’re welcome to join our open session on Friday, November 13, from 1–3PM PST, either in person or virtually. The agenda and registration information are available here.
Looking for other upcoming ethics events? You’ll find a list here.
Renee Knake Jefferson holds the endowed Doherty Chair in Legal Ethics and is a Professor of Law at the University of Houston. Check out more of her writing at the Legal Ethics Roundup. Find her on X (formerly Twitter) at @reneeknake or Bluesky at legalethics.bsky.social.
The post Legal Ethics Roundup: DOJ Ethics Probe, Bar Exam Tampering, AI Billing Limits, TX Reconsiders ABA Accreditation Council, Biglaw Shakeup, AI Privilege & More appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: John Fetterman And Other Losers On Election Day
articles.content:
I saw an opinion piece recently talking about the winners on Election Day: Decency, diversity, blah, blah, blah.
That’s doing things the easy way.
In this space, we do things the hard way.
Who were the biggest losers on Election Day?
Let’s start with John Fetterman, a Democratic senator who often supports Republican policies. If, as had been widely expected, the Democrats had won a narrow majority in the Senate — say, 51 or 52 seats — Fetterman would have been empowered. Like Joe Manchin five years ago, Fetterman’s one vote would have decided whether Democrats could pass bills. Fetterman would have had an awful lot of power.
Fetterman lost on Tuesday night.
With a multiseat majority, the Democrats can afford to lose Fetterman’s vote and still pass bills. In Congress, I like it when individual senators don’t have too much power. It’s better both for the senator’s massive ego and for America.
Who else lost on Election Day?
The far left of the Democratic Party.
My thinking here is the same as with Fetterman: With a slim majority, Democrats would need the votes of the far left fringe to pass any bills. With more seats in Democratic control, the centrists can pass laws without the support of a far left senator or two. That’s good; I’m glad it happened.
Other losers on Election Day?
Putin, thank God.
American can once again take Ukraine’s side in the war, resist Putin’s incursions on NATO, and impose sanctions as necessary. Presidents of course still have a lot of unilateral power in foreign affairs, but with large Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate, I’m hopeful that even lickspittle Republicans will remember that in the past they believed in a strong defense against Russia.
(It’s remarkable how people’s opinions change with the political winds. Within the next 10 years, I bet that the Southern Baptist Convention will again be telling me — as it did in the late 1990s, but did not in 2016 — that a president’s character matters. Never forget the hypocrisy of the Southern Baptist Convention.)
Is it also possible that sycophantic Republicans will rediscover that they believe in controlling the deficit, and free trade, and respect for the rule of law? As I’ve said before, I personally don’t care; Republican silence for the past 10 years has cost the party my vote in perpetuity. I just hope I have some good independents to vote for in the future, since I’m sure that the Democrats will soon disappoint me. (Don’t get me started on the financial condition of my home state of Illinois, where Democrats have controlled the state legislature for a couple of decades.)
Where was I?
Oh! Losers on Election Day.
Benjamin Netanyahu. A close relationship with Donald Trump was once an asset in Israel. Not so much any more, Bibi.
How about Iran?
Iran opposed Trump. Trump’s party lost. So Iran’s a winner, I guess.
But Trump knows that Congressional support for the war with Iran will go over a cliff in January, when the new Congress is sworn in. If Trump wants to make any military moves in Iran, he’s got two months to act. (I write these columns a couple of days before you read them. If the bombs are already falling in Iran when you are reading these words, that’s an issue of timing.)
Why would Trump bomb Iran between now and January? Does Trump really think he can trigger regime change in Iran with another few bombing runs? Does he think that a few more bombs will set back Iran’s nuclear program substantially further than where it is now? Does he think that restarting the war with Iran will help his domestic popularity?
I’m not sure that dropping more bombs on Iran will make any difference at this point, but it wouldn’t surprise me if Trump does it anyway. He’s promised to bomb, and he wants to blame the loss in Iran on Democrats (who, he’ll say, foolishly stopped his new bombing campaign just days before it would have succeeded).
If I had to predict, I’d say a few bombs will fall in November or December, followed by some kind of weird (and unhappy) peace next year. (The Democrats insist we should stop the war in Iran. But they’re far less loquacious when asked for details about what we should do. Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz. Iran may well start developing nukes. Do we just stop bombing? Do we negotiate something? What terms should we try to negotiate, and with what leverage? That’s a much harder issue than the campaign ads, which simply announce that we should, “Stop the war and reduce gas prices!”)
One last loser on Election Night: The Republican Party. The Republicans didn’t lose only because they lost the elections; Republicans lost because it’s now obvious that Trump never gave a damn about the Republican Party to begin with. If Trump had been on the ballot on Tuesday, he couldn’t possibly have lost; just ask him. The election would have been rigged! Trump would be screaming, “Election fraud!” and exhorting his followers to storm state and federal capitol buildings.
But Trump wasn’t on the ballot. Trump didn’t lose; other Republicans did. And Trump doesn’t give a damn about other Republicans.
Republicans sold their souls to Trump and he, in the end, deserted them.
Knock me over with a feather.
Mark Herrmann spent 17 years as a partner at a leading international law firm and later oversaw litigation, compliance and employment matters at a large international company. He is the author of The Curmudgeon’s Guide to Practicing Law and Drug and Device Product Liability Litigation Strategy (affiliate links). You can reach him by email at inhouse@abovethelaw.com.

articles.title: The Next Law School Admissions Crisis Could Be About Loans
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
It’ll take us a couple more years to see what kind of fallout in their ability to finance their education.
It’s anecdotal at this point, but you can see it coming. There’s a slice of students who don’t realize until they’re through the application, admission, and matriculation process what that full picture looks like for them. Many know the cost, but they haven’t really delved into what that looks like. Maybe they’ve walked an unconventional path to get to law school, and their credit is not where they are able to access private loans. That brings a challenge, so they could end up deferring or wondering whether legal education is right for them.
— Sudha Setty, president and CEO of the Law School Admission Council, discussing the potential impact of changes to graduate student lending in an interview with the ABA Journal. The new rules ended Grad PLUS loans for new borrowers starting July 1, 2026. JD students borrowing for the first time after that date can access up to $50,000 a year in federal loans, subject to a $200,000 lifetime cap. Students who need more may have to turn to private lenders, where eligibility depends on credit history, and private loans aren’t eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness.
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
